<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S7" title="In MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">7 </span>Conclusion</span></a></li>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2604.08516v1/icon.svg" id="g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:26/26;" width="26" height="26"></object></span>
<span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Web agents—autonomous systems that navigate and execute tasks on the web on behalf of users—have the potential to transform how people interact with the digital world. However, the most capable web agents today rely on proprietary models with undisclosed training data and recipes, limiting scientific understanding, reproducibility, and community-driven progress.
We believe agents for the open web should be built in the open. To this end, we introduce (1) <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span>, a large and diverse mixture of browser task demonstrations and web-GUI perception data and (2) <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> a family of fully open multimodal web agents.
Specifically, <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> combines over 100K synthetic task trajectories from multiple complementary generation pipelines with 30K<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>+</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+</annotation></semantics></math> human demonstrations, atomic web-skill trajectories, and GUI perception data, including referring expression grounding and screenshot question answering. <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agents operate as instruction-conditioned visual-language action policies: given a task instruction and a webpage screenshot, they predict the next browser action, requiring no access to HTML, accessibility trees, or specialized APIs.
Available in 4B and 8B size, on browser-use benchmarks like <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span>, <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Online-Mind2Web</span>, and <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DeepShop</span>, <span id="abstract1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agents achieve state-of-the-art results outperforming similar scale open-weight-only models such as Fara-7B, UI-Tars-1.5-7B, and Holo1-7B. <span id="abstract1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-8B also surpasses set-of-marks (SoM) agents built on much larger closed frontier models like GPT-4o. We further demonstrate consistent gains through test-time scaling via parallel rollouts with best-of-N selection, achieving 94.7% and 60.5% pass@4 (compared to 78.2% and 35.3% pass@1)on <span id="abstract1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> and <span id="abstract1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Online-Mind2Web</span> respectively. We will release model checkpoints, training data, code, and a unified evaluation harness to enable reproducibility and accelerate open research on web agents.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.08516v1/Model_inference_3.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/261;" width="381" height="261" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of <span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>.<span id="S1.F1.5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> At each step, the agent receives the task instruction, current screenshot, and action history as input. It then predicts a natural language thought followed by a browser action.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.08516v1/teaser_5.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/372;" width="381" height="372" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of <span id="S1.F2.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> dataset.<span id="S1.F2.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> To capture the diverse capabilities required for web agents, <span id="S1.F2.9.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> combines GUI perception data involving screenshot QA </span>(top left)<span id="S1.F2.9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> and referring expression grounding </span>(top right)<span id="S1.F2.9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">, with synthetic and human task trajectories demonstrating task completion on the web </span>(bottom)<span id="S1.F2.9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. The human trajectories are further segmented into atomic skills (<a href="#S2.T1" title="In 2.2 Atomic skill trajectories ‣ 2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows our skill taxonomy).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The World Wide Web is an indispensable part of modern human life, with billions of people relying on it daily for information, communication, commerce, and entertainment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>. From booking flights and managing finances to navigating government services, comparison shopping, and coordinating logistics, countless everyday tasks require users to interact with complex, multi-step web interfaces that demand sustained attention, domain knowledge, and patience <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>. Web agents—autonomous systems that can navigate and execute such tasks on the web at the behest of users <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>—have the potential to fundamentally reshape how humans interact with this vast digital ecosystem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>.
Effective web agents could broaden digital access for users who face barriers due to disability or inaccessible design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, as well as for users with limited digital skills or digital literacy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent progress in large language and vision-language models has brought web agents closer to practical viability, supported by research benchmarks demonstrating multi-step web interaction (e.g., clicking, form filling, and navigation) under natural-language instructions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>.
In parallel, frontier labs now expose computer- or browser-use capabilities where models perceive GUI state via screenshots and output low-level actions such as click/type/scroll to complete workflows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.
However, the most capable end-to-end systems are typically offered as hosted, proprietary services with limited disclosure of training data and full recipes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.
This exacerbates long-standing concerns that insufficient reporting and artifacts hinder reproducibility and scientific understanding of what actually drives performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>.
The resulting opacity is especially concerning for autonomous agents operating on the open web, where trustworthy deployment depends on transparency, accountability, and auditable behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">We believe agents for the open web should be built in the open.</span>
To this end, we provide the research community with a complete, transparent, and reproducible foundation including: <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span>, a mixture of diverse task demonstrations on the browser and web-GUI perception data (Sec. <a href="#S2" title="2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>); and <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>, a family of fully open and efficient multimodal web agents (Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 MolmoWeb ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). <span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agents are vision-language models (VLMs) trained to serve as instruction-conditioned multimodal action policies for the web. Given a task instruction, action history, and a screenshot of the webpage, <span id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agent predicts the next browser action. The action is executed in the browser to yield a new observation and this loop repeats until the task is complete.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Crucially, <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agents operate on any website using only the visual interface that human users see, without requiring specialized APIs or access to the underlying HTML or accessibility tree (AxTree). This vision-centric design is a deliberate choice motivated by several considerations. First, it mirrors how people actually use the web, grounding the agent in the same perceptual modality and making its behavior more interpretable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Second, it avoids the brittleness of Document Object Model (DOM) based representations, which vary significantly across websites, frameworks, and even minor page updates, and which can be incomplete or misleading for dynamically rendered content. Third, it sidesteps the substantial token consumption and compute overhead that structured page representations incur: AxTree inputs can easily consume tens of thousands of tokens per page, whereas a single screenshot provides a compact, information-rich representation of the same content.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The key to training capable <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agents is curating a high-quality and diverse training data mixture that simultaneously teaches the model to understand web screenshots as well as task execution behaviors, such as filling forms, multi-hop navigation, and finding relevant information from a webpage. <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> contains data from four complementary data sources: (1) synthetic task trajectories generated at scale from multiple complementary pipelines, (2) human demonstrations collected by crowdworkers on real websites, (3) atomic web skill trajectories providing targeted supervision for compositional browser-use skills, and (4) GUI perception data consisting of referring expression grounding and screenshot question-answering examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Despite their relatively compact size at 4B or 8B scale, <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agents are highly performant. <span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Without distilling from other visual web agents</span>, <span id="S1.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agents are competitive with or outperform open-weights agents of comparable size, including Fara-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> and Holo1-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>.
More notably, they also outperform set-of-marks (SoM) prompting based web agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite> built on much larger closed frontier models like GPT-4o that take both AxTree and SoM-annotated screenshots as inputs.
This result is particularly striking because these closed-model baselines enjoy substantially richer input representations <em id="S1.p7.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">and</em> orders-of-magnitude more parameters, yet a well-trained, vision-only <span id="S1.p7.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agent achieves stronger task completion rates—suggesting that data quality and targeted training can compensate for raw model scale and additional inputs.
Finally, we demonstrate further gains by leveraging increased compute at inference-time via multiple rollouts with best outcome selection using a VLM judge.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span></h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our training data consists of 3 broad categories: task trajectories, atomic skill trajectories, and GUI perception data. The trajectory generation pipeline encompasses web browsing task sampling, trajectory execution, and filtering out failed trajectories, as shown in <a href="#S2.F3" title="In 2.1 Task trajectories ‣ 2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Task trajectories</h3>

<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.08516v1/Datagen_2.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/192;" width="471" height="192" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Data generation pipeline<span id="S2.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. Our pipeline consists of a task sampler, trajectory generation executed by either humans or AxTree agents, and success filtering.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectories from AxTree agents.</span>
A bulk of our synthetic trajectories are generated using an LLM agent that operates on the AxTree representation of the webpage. At each step, the agent receives the serialized AxTree (visualized in <a href="#S2.F3" title="In 2.1 Task trajectories ‣ 2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) as its observation along with the instruction and past actions, and predicts the next action by referencing element browser IDs (<span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">bid</span>) assigned to each interactive node. We used Gemini-3-Flash-Preview as the agent backbone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Tasks were sourced from a combination of manually authored and LLM-generated instructions, covering popular websites and benchmark evaluation sites (see <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Synthetic Trajectories Generation ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> in the Appendix for details). Although the agent observes only the AxTree, we capture a screenshot at each step so that all trajectories share a unified observation format. Actions predicted in bid-space are post-processed into pixel-space coordinates (clicks, typing, scrolling). See <a href="#S3.T3" title="In 3.2 Observation and action space ‣ 3 MolmoWeb ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>
for the complete list of actions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Synthetic trajectories were filtered for task success using the WebVoyager LLM judge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, retaining only trajectories deemed successfully completed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectories from multiagent harness.</span>
To generate trajectories with potentially a higher quality of thoughts and trajectories, we design a multi-agent system (<a href="#S2.F4" title="In 2.1 Task trajectories ‣ 2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) where the the system orchestrates web navigation through three specialized roles working in concert: a <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Planner</span> generates the immediate next subgoal based on the high-level task goal as well as task progress determined from verification feedback; an <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Operator</span> executes one low-level browser action (like clicking, scrolling etc.) at each step to accomplish the current subgoal; and a <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Verifier</span> checks whether the current subgoal has been completed by analyzing the most recent 5 screenshots. The trajectory generation process operates iteratively. At each step, the system first runs the <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Verifier</span> to check if the current subgoal is complete. If the subgoal is verified as complete or fails to complete within 5 steps, the <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Planner</span> is called to generate the next subgoal. The system then injects the current subgoal, completed steps, and planner/verifier reasoning into the text prompt and passes this augmented prompt along with the current screenshot to the <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Operator</span>, which returns a concrete browser action. Finally, all historical information is tracked and fed back into subsequent planning and execution cycles. We use Gemini-2.5-Flash for the <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Planner</span>, GPT4-o as the <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Verifier</span>, and Gemini AxTree agent as the Operator. We empirically find that this multi-agent setup achieves higher task completion success rates than using the Gemini AxTree agent alone, scoring 78.5 vs. 74.4 on <span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.08516v1/multiagent_trajectories_0.png" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/115;" width="381" height="115" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S2.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Multi-agent trajectory generation pipeline.<span id="S2.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> A Planner decomposes the task into sequential subgoals. For each subgoal, an Operator generates an action conditioned on the current state and subgoal. After execution, the resulting state is evaluated by a Verifier using screenshots to determine whether the subgoal is achieved. If not, the system continues attempting the same subgoal; otherwise, the Planner generates the next one. The loop repeats until the overall goal is completed.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectories from humans.</span>
In addition to the synthetic trajectories, we collected human demonstrations via a custom Chrome extension that captures browser interaction events (e.g., clicks, scrolls, keystrokes) and corresponding screenshots, and post-processes them into standardized trajectories. Crowdworkers were provided with tasks sourced from a mix of manually authored and LLM-generated instructions (see <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Human Trajectory Annotation ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> in the Appendix for details). In general, tasks were chosen to span a wide range of popular websites and to require a variety of browser task-completion skills including search, form-filling, and multi-hop navigation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To support fine-grained annotation, each task instruction was decomposed into an ordered sequence of subtasks. Workers checked off each subtask upon completion within the annotation tool and submitted a final text response (e.g., an answer to a question or a completion acknowledgment). If a subtask could not be completed due to missing content or an unexpected webpage state, workers recorded their best attempt along with a descriptive note explaining the failure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Each trajectory is reviewed by a human to verify task completion and ensure that screenshots and actions were correctly captured. Trajectories failing review were revised or re-collected.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectories from node traversal.</span>
To complement LLM and human generated task-completion trajectories with verifiable, deterministic supervision, we construct navigation trajectories from precomputed website graphs. We first build a directed graph over 500 popular websites via breadth-first exploration: starting from the homepage, we extract the accessibility tree at each page and prompt an LLM to select a diverse set of navigational links (e.g., category pages, search features, content sections), continuing to a depth of four. Root-to-leaf paths through each graph yield URL sequences that serve as ground-truth navigation plans, as shown in <a href="#S2.F5" title="In 2.1 Task trajectories ‣ 2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.08516v1/nodetraversal_3.png" id="S2.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/181;" width="429" height="181" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S2.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Node traversal trajectory generation pipeline.<span id="S2.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Starting from a website’s homepage, we extract all reachable URLs and use an LLM to select the most informative ones for breadth-first expansion, pruning cycles to avoid loops. A deterministic, LLM-free procedure then generates trajectories by traversing the resulting paths via scrolling and clicking, with success verified through URL matching. Each validated trajectory is paired with an LLM-generated goal conditioned on the full trajectory, producing a task consistent with the produced path.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">To convert a chosen sequence of URLs in the node-graph to a trajectory, we use a deterministic process that does not rely on an LLM to replay each path using browser actions like clicking and scrolling. Starting at the root URL, we locates the link to the next target in the accessibility tree, scroll if necessary to bring it into view, and click. Because the agent uses no language model at execution time, trajectories are cheap to produce at scale, and the intended route is known <em id="S2.SS1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">a priori</em>, enabling straightforward success verification. When the agent cannot reach a target URL, the path is truncated to the last successfully visited page. At the terminal page of each trajectory, we use an LLM to generate a plausible instruction. Together the instruction-trajectory pair generated via a walk on the node-graph now resembles a goal-directed browser demonstration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Atomic skill trajectories</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While task trajectories require the agent to compose multiple web skills to complete an end-to-end goal (like searching for a product, applying filters, and adding to cart; each requiring a sequence of low-level browser actions), atomic skill trajectories isolate individual skills. We identify a core taxonomy of web skills that underlie most browsing tasks, including search, form filling, finding an element or information on page, and filtering (see <a href="#S2.T1" title="In 2.2 Atomic skill trajectories ‣ 2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Providing targeted supervision for each skill ensures the model develops reliable competence in these building blocks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S2.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.T1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Taxonomy of atomic web skills used in human annotation.</span></figcaption>

<tr id="S2.T1.6.10" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="S2.T1.6.12.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.T1.6.12.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Free-form navigation when stepwise decomposition is unknown</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Extracted from human trajectories.</span>
Because human task trajectories were annotated with ordered subtask decompositions, each subtask segment naturally constitutes an atomic skill trajectory. Specifically, each segment begins from the browser state in which the previous subtask ended, and carries the subtask instruction as its goal. We automatically extract these segments from the full human trajectories, yielding short, focused demonstrations. Since skill segments within a trajectory begin from the browser state where the last skill segment ends, these demonstrations resemble response to a follow-up query to the user’s previous query. Therefore, this data might also enable the agent to learn multi-turn interaction with the user.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generated by an AxTree agent.</span>
To supplement the extracted segments, we additionally prompted the AxTree agent to execute targeted skill instructions for two important skills: <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fill_form</span> and <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">find_and_open</span>. For each, instructions were of the form “<span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">go to:[URL]\n fill form:[form details]</span>” or “<span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">go to:[URL]\n find and open:[target]</span>.” This directly yields skill-level trajectories without requiring segmentation of longer task trajectories.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span><span id="S2.T2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Statistics of <span id="S2.T2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span></span>. We also report its constituent sources compared to other datasets.</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>GUI perception</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Effective web navigation requires the agent to perceive and understand webpage screenshots before taking any action. GUI perception data teaches the model to identify interactive elements on the page (e.g., buttons, links, input fields, and other controls), understand their function and affordances, and extract information from the page in response to natural language queries. This combines skills akin to referring expression grounding, OCR, and reading comprehension, grounded in the visual structure of web interfaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Grounding.</span>
Grounding data consists of (screenshot, element description) <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> click point pairs, where the model must predict the pixel coordinate to click for interacting with a specified element. We extract these pairs automatically from AxTree agent trajectories. For each screenshot, we enumerate all clickable elements in the AxTree and for each generate a natural language description using its accessible name and role either with a template or GPT5. The ground-truth click coordinate is sampled randomly within the element’s bounding box using a clipped Gaussian prior centered at the element’s center, encouraging the model to learn spatially robust clicking rather than always targeting exact centers. In total, we generate more than 7M grounding QA pairs, comprising 3.4M templated queries and 3.8M GPT-5-generated queries.
In addition to new grounding data, we also repurpose the PixmoPoints data from Molmo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> by formatting single-point QA pairs into click actions and include 1.1M examples in our grounding mixture.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Screenshot QA.</span>
Screenshot QA data consists of (screenshot, question) <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math> answer pairs that enhance the model’s ability to read and reason about webpage content. For each screenshot in a subset of the AxTree agent trajectories, we provide the corresponding AxTree to an LLM and prompt it to generate question–answer pairs. Questions cover three categories: OCR queries about text and values present on the page (e.g., prices, counts, text content), affordance queries about actions available on the page (e.g., “Where would I find financial news on this page?”), and summarization queries about the overall content or purpose of a page element. To ensure that questions and answers rely solely on visual content, we remove samples that contain references to AxTree-specific information, such as element IDs (e.g., “Click on Bid 32”). In total, the dataset covers 395 websites and 2,237,252 QA pairs, split between 54% OCR, 26% affordance, and 20% summarization questions.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we describe the <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> architecture, its observation and action space, and the training procedure. <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> is designed to be simple and practical: we build on an existing vision-language model backbone, define a minimal but expressive action space over browser operations, and train end-to-end via supervised fine-tuning on the <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> mixture.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Architecture</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> is built on the Molmo2 architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, a multimodal language model that processes interleaved sequences of images and text. As shown in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the model takes as input the current webpage screenshot together with the task instruction and the history of past actions, and produces a structured output comprising a natural language thought followed by the next action to execute.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Observation and action space</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observations.</span>
At each step <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the model receives a screenshot of the current browser viewport along with the task instruction. To provide temporal context, the history of actions taken in 10 prior steps is appended as context along with the URL and title of the current page.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Actions.</span> The model predicts a JSON object encoding both a <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">thought</em> and an <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">action</em> specifying the operation to perform. The thought is a brief natural language rationale for the chosen action. The full action space is described in <a href="#S3.T3" title="In 3.2 Observation and action space ‣ 3 MolmoWeb ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Mouse actions are parameterized by spatial coordinates normalized to <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,100]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,100</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,100]</annotation></semantics></math>, with 2 decimal points, which are denormalized to viewport pixel coordinates at execution time.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.T3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Action space of <span id="S3.T3.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>.<span id="S3.T3.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Spatial coordinates are normalized to <math id="S3.T3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,100]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,100</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,100]</annotation></semantics></math> during training and denormalized to viewport pixels for browser execution. <a href="#A3.F8" title="In C.1.1 Manually written task templates. ‣ C.1 Task Sampling ‣ Appendix C Synthetic Trajectories Generation ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> in the Appendix shows the distribution of actions in various subsets of <span id="S3.T3.6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span>.</span></span></figcaption>
<table id="S3.T3.7" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.T3.7.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T3.7.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.7pt 4.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T3.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:144.9pt;">
<span id="S3.T3.7.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.T3.7.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Action</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T3.7.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.7pt 4.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T3.7.1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:172.5pt;">
<span id="S3.T3.7.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.T3.7.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Description</span></span>

<tr id="S3.T3.7.2" class="ltx_tr">

<tr id="S3.T3.7.3" class="ltx_tr">

</span></td>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Training</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> end-to-end via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on all training data described in <a href="#S2" title="2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. All data types, including task trajectories, atomic skill trajectories, and GUI perception data, are mixed in a single training stage. The mixing ratios across data sources are treated as hyperparameters; we ablate different mixtures and select the combination that best balances performance across evaluation benchmarks. We report the datasets’ final ratios in the mixture in Table <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.2 Atomic skill trajectories ‣ 2 MolmoWebMix ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We finetune Molmo2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> (with Qwen3 language model and SigLIP2 vision encoder) following its best practice and tune the language model, the vision encoder, and the adapter starting from the single-image checkpoint (pretrained on image captioning and finetuned on single-image QA). We train all models with 64 H100 GPUs with a global batch size of 128 for up to 50K steps (approximately 3.2 epochs on average, with slightly different numbers of epochs across datasets based on their final ratio in the mixture).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments consist of comparison to prior art, a study on scaling test-time compute through more inference steps per rollout as well as parallel rollouts with best-of-N selection, data ablation studies to understand the impact of scale and role of human vs synthetic data, comparison of token sampling strategies, and grounding evaluation. We first describe our evaluation setup and then present our experimental results.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T4.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.T4.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison to prior work on browser-use benchmarks.<span id="S4.T4.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> For models marked with a *, the numbers reported are from Fara <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. Italic <span id="S4.T4.10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Online-Mind2Web</span> results are from the Online-Mind2Web auto-eval leaderboard. Since its unclear what judge was used by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> for <span id="S4.T4.10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebTailBench</span> we used the <span id="S4.T4.10.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> judge to compute numbers marked with †. We highlight the </span>best<span id="S4.T4.10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> and <span id="S4.T4.10.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">second-best</span> performing numbers for each benchmark in the sub-8B, open-weight model category.</span></span></figcaption>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Evaluation setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> on four popular web browsing benchmarks using live websites: <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Online-Mind2Web</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DeepShop</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, and <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebTailBench</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. Because some tasks are time-sensitive, we change dates in outdated requests (e.g., find a flight on August 5, 2025) to be meaningful for the task across all benchmarks. For each benchmark and model, we run 3-5 evaluations up to 100 steps and report the average score across runs. If a model does not complete the task by the maximum number of steps, it is considered a failure. As environment errors occasionally occur, we allow up to 10 retries per trajectory; tasks that do not complete within this budget are also marked as failures. We use the same prompt and LLM-as-a-judge setup corresponding to each published benchmark. Specifically, we use GPT-4o with the official prompt from <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DeepShop</span>, and o4-mini with respective judge for <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Online-Mind2Web</span>. Since, it is unclear what judge was used for <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebTailBench</span>, we used the <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> judge. For <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span>, we use the task set provided by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> which removed infeasible tasks. All evaluations are run in a Browserbase environment, allowing many live browsers to run in parallel with some captcha-solving capability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Comparison to prior work</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Tab. <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we compare <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> to web-agents based on proprietary APIs as well as open-weight models.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> establishes a new state-of-the-art among open-weight models.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-8B shows healthy gains over leading open-weight models like Fara across all benchmarks. Even <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-4B outperforms all open-weight models on <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DeepShop</span> while being competitive on <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Online-Mind2Web</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebTailBench</span>. These gains largely demonstrate efficacy of <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> in teaching a strong foundation vision-language model like <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Molmo2</span> to follow instructions for browser-task completion.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Comparison to closed visual agents.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to SoM agents that use set-of-marks annotated visual prompts, <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-8B easily outperforms GPT-4o, matches the performance of o3 on <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span>, and is only 6 pts behind GPT-5 and o3 on <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DeepShop</span>. <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-8B also outperforms OpenAI computer-use-preview on <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DeepShop</span> as per the performance reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Comparison to non-visual teacher agent.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our synthetic data generation pipeline is powered by Gemini-3-flash axtree agent. It is natural to ask how does the visual student, <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>, fair against the non-visual axtree-guided teacher? <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-8B agent is <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5+</annotation></semantics></math> pts behind the teacher on <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Online-Mind2Web</span> while being <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10+</annotation></semantics></math> pts behind on <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DeepShop</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebTailBench</span>. Besides the observation space, other factors contributing to this gap include: (i) differences in model sizes with Gemini presumably being a much larger model compared to our humble 4B and 8B models); (ii) click action requires pixel-space pointing capability from <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> but the Axtree agent uses unique numeric identifiers (<code id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">bid</code> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>) of the target element which is then programmatically mapped to a click location; and (iii) answering questions based on text rendered on the webpage requires <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> to implicitly perform OCR to parse text from screenshot in addition to reading comprehension required by the Axtree agent.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Test-time scaling</h3>

<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2604.08516v1/pass_at_ks.svg" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/183;" width="476" height="183"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F6.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F6.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Pass@k performance on <span id="S4.F6.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> and <span id="S4.F6.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Online-Mind2Web</span><span id="S4.F6.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Accuracy improves as k increases, with <span id="S4.F6.8.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-8B generally outperforming <span id="S4.F6.8.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-4B, and 100 steps outperforming 30 steps by a large margin. The <span id="S4.F6.8.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-8B model with max 100 steps reaches 94.7% and 60.5% at Pass@4.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We explore two ways of utilizing more compute at inference time: (i) performing parallel rollouts with a best-of-N selection with an LLM-judge; and (ii) increasing the number of inference steps.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Parallel rollouts.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study how much performance can be gained by running <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> independent agents on the same task and selecting the best outcome.
To get an unbiased, low variance estimate of pass@<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, we collect <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m&gt;k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m&gt;k</annotation></semantics></math> rollouts per task and compute the estimate:</p>
<table id="S4.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\text{pass@}k}=1-\frac{\binom{m-c}{k}}{\binom{m}{k}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mtext>pass@</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\text{pass@}k}=1-\frac{\binom{m-c}{k}}{\binom{m}{k}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of successful rollouts among the <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> attempts. We use an LLM judge to evaluate success for each rollout, and we set <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=5</annotation></semantics></math> to balance accuracy with computational cost. We plot <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-4B and <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-8B’s pass@k performance on the <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebVoyager</span> benchmark with max steps of 30 and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=1,...,4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=1,...,4</annotation></semantics></math> in Fig. <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.3 Test-time scaling ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> using the respective judge for best rollout selection. We see that for both 4B and 8B models, parallel rollouts improve success rates substantially with pass@<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> leading to 20+ pt gains over single rollout performance. Parallel rollouts help mitigate the compounding error problem where a single incorrect action could throw the agent off-course. These massive gains from parallel rollouts suggest (or, perhaps explain to the unsurprised why) self-distillation from best-of-N rollouts and RL might be effective strategies for further improving single rollout performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Increasing inference steps.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.3 Test-time scaling ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows consistent gain from increasing the maximum number of inference steps from 30 to 100 across all benchmarks. However, we note that the gains from scaling via parallel runs (each with 30 steps) and picking the best result using an LLM judge far outperform increasing the number of inference steps (e.g., 8B model achieves <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="86.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>86.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">86.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> via 3 parallel runs with max 30 steps resulting in a total of 90 steps compared to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="78.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>78.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">78.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> via increasing the steps to 100 in one run).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Training data ablations</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S4.T5" title="In Limited gains from human data on benchmarks. ‣ 4.4 Training data ablations ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we evaluate the effect of data scale and contributions from synthetic and human data to final performance. The ablations used a slightly earlier version of <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> which had fewer human trajectories as well as fewer synthetic trajectories but largely had a similar composition to the final version of <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Performance improves with training data scale.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T5.sf1" title="In Table 5 ‣ Limited gains from human data on benchmarks. ‣ 4.4 Training data ablations ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5a</span></a> shows that, unsurprisingly, performance improves with data scale. Interestingly, about <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>85</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">85</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the performance can be achieved with just <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the dataset highlighting the effectiveness of the training mixture.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limited gains from human data on benchmarks.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T5.sf2" title="In Table 5 ‣ Limited gains from human data on benchmarks. ‣ 4.4 Training data ablations ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5b</span></a> shows that gains from human data are somewhat limited and not consistent across benchmarks. This is likely due to lower volume of human data, differences in task distribution compared to benchmarks, difficulty in learning new actions present only in human data (<span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll_at</span> and <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mouse_drag_and_drop</span>), difference in style and quality of post-hoc generated thoughts, and human annotation noise (e.g. variable scroll amounts in human annotation as opposed to always scrolling by 100% of viewport height in synthetic data). We hypothesize that synthetic and human data represent distinctly different web task completion policies and the model struggles to learn generalizable behavior across both. For instance, while we observe the model trained only on human data produces both <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll</span> and <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll_at</span> actions, when trained along with synthetic trajectories the model almost always produces <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll</span> which tries to scroll the page instead of the element.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.T5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Data ablations<span id="S4.T5.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. These ablations use an earlier version of <span id="S4.T5.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> with both fewer synthetic and human trajectories compared to the final experiments and use 30 inference steps.</span></span></figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<td id="S4.T5.sf2.5.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">21.4</td></tr>

</figure></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Synthetic trajectories are more effective for learning than human trajectories for the same tasks.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further investigate the difference in learning from trajectories collected by AxTree agents and humans, we collect 2700 web browsing trajectories with each method, using the same task instructions. We then train the model on each of these datasets, mixed with <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span>-Perception data. <a href="#S4.T6" title="In Synthetic trajectories are more effective for learning than human trajectories for the same tasks. ‣ 4.4 Training data ablations ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows that the model trained on AxTree-sourced trajectories consistently outperforms the one trained on human trajectories, suggesting that the synthetic data provides a more reliable learning signal. We hypothesize two contributing factors for higher signal-to-noise ratio in synthetic trajectories. First, humans tend to exhibit more exploratory behavior, particularly on unfamiliar websites, resulting in longer and noisier trajectories with detours that may hinder imitation learning. Second, the LLM agent operates on the accessibility tree, which encodes rich structural and semantic information about page elements that may not be immediately apparent from visual cues alone. This additional context likely enables the LLM to produce more direct and consistent trajectories, making them more effective as training data despite being synthetically generated.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.T6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Learning from LLM-generated trajectories is more effective than learning from human demonstrations.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Sampling Strategies</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T7" title="In 4.5 Sampling Strategies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> compares greedy, top-k, and top-p (nucleus) sampling on <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebV</span>. We find that sampling strategy significantly affects <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>’s performance, achieving over 5% gains with top-k and top-p sampling compared to greedy decoding. Qualitatively, we find the greedy-decoding could get stuck at specific states (e.g. trying to click at the same location or continuing to scroll even when past attempts at doing so have failed), while the other randomized strategies overcome this behavior. Between top-k and top-p sampling, we see that nucleus sampling with p=0.8 and temperature=0.7 performs the best on Webvoyager and hence is the default sampling strategy used for all experiments. We choose the sampling parameters based on Qwen3’s (the base LLM used in <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Molmo2</span>) recommended parameters on HuggingFace <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 7</span>: </span><span id="S4.T7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Effect of sampling strategy.<span id="S4.T7.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Greedy sampling performs significantly worse than random sampling strategies.</span></span></figcaption>
<table id="S4.T7.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T7.6.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T7.6.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt">Strategy</td>
<td id="S4.T7.6.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T7.6.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WebV</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T7.6.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T7.6.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">greedy (temperature=0.0)</td>
<td id="S4.T7.6.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">61.4</td></tr>

</section>
