<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S4.T8" title="In 4.6 Grounding Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, we evaluate <span id="S4.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-Ground-8B—an 8B grounding specialist trained only on grounding data as well as the <span id="S4.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-4B agent on two grounding benchmarks: ScreenSpot <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> and ScreenSpot v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>. We see that the grounding specialist outperforms open-weight models as well as much larger proprietary models like Claude 3.7 and OpenAI CUA. Our humble <span id="S4.SS6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>-4B agent is only a few points behind the specialist grounding model while gaining competence on web task completion in addition to grounding.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now review related work on GUI understanding, different kinds of web agents, and evaluation benchmarks for web agents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM-driven web agents.</span> Given the generalizable reasoning skills demonstrated by modern LLMs, many works have explored using an LLM as the core reasoning engine for a web agent, often employing prompting frameworks like ReAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite> that interleave reasoning and action steps. This bifurcates into two broad approaches: (1) using an LLM to directly operate on a language representation of the web page derived from the DOM (such as the accessibility tree representation) to predict browser interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, or (2) exposing web capabilities via API-based tools (e.g. using search engine APIs or other website specific APIs) to a tool-use or coding agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>. While this approach works well for specific use cases where the APIs are available and known a priori, it lacks the generality of directly operating the browser as a human would, which unlocks the full range of economically useful tasks on the web. Other work has explored fine-tuning LLMs on web interaction data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, multi-agent orchestration frameworks that decompose web tasks across specialized agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, and tree search methods for planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal web agents.</span> In contrast, there are increasing efforts to build agents that process screenshots to produce actions. Earlier work in this direction involved creating modular systems involving planning, grounding, and verification modules <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite> or training dedicated visual language models for GUI interaction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite>. Recent work focuses more on a unified approach using a VLM to output actions given screenshot, instruction, and action history. This includes proprietary closed models like Gemini and OpenAI computer-use models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, and a handful of open-weights-only models like Fara <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, UI-Tars family of models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>, Holo-1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, and OpenCUA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>. Others have explored reinforcement learning with search for web agent training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>. Unfortunately, without fully open training data and transparent training and evaluation pipelines, it’s impossible to advance the science of these multimodal agentic systems. Our work aims to fill this gap with our fully open training dataset <span id="S5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span>, training and evaluation pipelines, and weights for our 4B and 8B <span id="S5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> models. It is also worth noting that, unlike prior work such as Fara, we avoid distillation from proprietary vision-based web agents. Our data pipeline largely relies on human trajectories and synthetic trajectories generated from AxTree agents that do not see screenshots.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GUI understanding.</span> Separate from applications to web agents, many works have looked at the GUI parsing tasks in isolation, including GUI referring expression grounding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>, answering questions about screenshots, and parsing screenshots into structured representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite>. While we use GUI grounding and QA data as sources of auxiliary supervision, our primary goal is to learn to follow instructions to solve tasks on the web.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation of web agents.</span> Evaluating web agents is challenging. Early evaluation work focused on sandboxed web environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, desktop environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>, and multi-turn dialogue navigation datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> where the answer is known or verifiable using oracle knowledge of environment state. Recently, several benchmarks have proposed evaluating on live websites. While some use automatic verifiers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> or simple text answers that are unlikely to change over time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite>, other use a VLM-as-a-judge to verify task completion correctness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>. A VLM-judge (typically a frontier model such as GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>) takes the instruction, screenshots, and the final answer produced by the agent, along with a prompt specifying the success criteria, and outputs a success or failure decision, along with a rationale for that decision.
Online-Mind2Web <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite> proposes a more thorough judge that first prompts an LLM to identify key requirements for the successful completion of the task, then identifies key screenshots, and then focuses only on these key screenshots to make the final judgment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Capabilities and Limitations</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now discuss the capabilities and limitations of <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> along various dimensions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S6.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Instruction following:</span> <span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> was trained with a wide range of instructions across different levels of specificity. The agent performs best for more specific instructions but performance may degrade as the instructions become more ambiguous or require more exploration. <span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> may work best when the name or URL of the target website is mentioned in the instruction. <span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> may also struggle to follow instructions with many constraints or search filters.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OCR and reading comprehension:</span> To answer questions about the current screenshot (e.g., a question pertaining to a paragraph visible in the screenshot), the agent needs to not only localize the relevant part of the webpage, but also implicitly perform OCR and reading comprehension. <span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> is surprisingly capable at this challenging task, but we do see instances of failures due to OCR for smaller texts or for answering complex questions requiring understanding of large passages of text.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Latency:</span> <span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> is trained on trajectories that aim to be efficient and minimize the number of actions required to accomplish the task. However, the model is not optimized for latency (i.e., model feedforward inference time per step). Feedforward efficiency may further be optimized through techniques like quantization or pruning. Another latency bottleneck is the time it takes for the action to be executed in the browser. Browser action execution is faster for local browsers than hosted browsers like Browserbase (especially with proxy configurations), but the latter allows effortless scaling to many concurrent sessions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Thoughts:</span> An interesting capability by virtue of producing thoughts is that <span id="S6.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> can sometimes use thoughts as memory for storing information during the trajectory and reference it for producing the final answer (since past thoughts and actions are provided as context at every step). For instance, when asked to list top news headlines, the agent would keep track of all headlines via thoughts as it scrolls through the news headlines list. However, does not demonstrate this behavior robustly. We also see failure modes where thoughts sometimes do not correlate well with actions. For instance, the thought might say the agent needs to type some text and press Enter but the action is directly to press Enter.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action space:</span> <span id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> uses the action space that humans use when interacting with GUIs. Combining some of these actions could yield shorter trajectories. For example, for searching a query with a search box, <span id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> currently clicks to select the input box, uses a <code id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">keyboard_type</code> action, and then either uses <code id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">keyboard_press(`Enter')</code> or clicks on the search button to execute the search. This sequence could be combined into a single <code id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">type_at(text,x,y,press_enter=True)</code> action. Another potentially useful action not currently included is <code id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.7" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">web_search(query)</code> that directly passes query arguments to a search engine via URL parameters (e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> may benefit from this action). <span id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> struggles with predicting more infrequent actions like <span id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll_at</span>, <span id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mouse_drag_and_drop</span>, or <span id="S6.I1.i5.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">hover</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error correction and restarts:</span> While <span id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> shows some error correction behavior (e.g., using the <code id="S6.I1.i6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">go_back</code> action or scrolling to the top of the page if the agent did not find the information on scrolling down), the agent may sometimes get stuck in states where it incorrectly keeps predicting the same action (eg. repeatedly scrolling or clicking at the same location) without being able to recover or course-correct.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span> and <span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>, a fully open data and model suite for multimodal web agents. Operating purely from screenshots, <span id="S7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span> agents outperform both comparable open-weight models and set-of-marks agents built on much larger proprietary models, while benefiting from test-time scaling via parallel rollouts. We’ll release all checkpoints, data, code, and evaluation tools to support reproducible research and accelerate progress on open web agents.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Author Contributions</h3>

<div id="S7.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tanmay Gupta, Piper Wolters, Zixian Ma and Peter Sushko collectively contributed to dataset construction, model training, and conducted numerous exploratory experiments for this project.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SSx1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tanmay Gupta</span> conceptualized and led the project. He worked with all contributors to provide directional guidance, ideate, plan, and debug. Tanmay contributed code to all aspects of <span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWeb</span>–data collection, training, and evaluation. He also wrote the initial versions of synthetic data generation and evaluation harnesses, created the task generation pipeline for human data annotation, and coordinated with Snorkel AI throughout the human trajectory annotation effort. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Piper Wolters</span> led the development and integration of the project’s core infrastructure, spanning human data collection, synthetic data generation, environment setup, model training, evaluation, and the demo. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zixian Ma</span> led model training, grounding, and multi-agent synthetic trajectories. She generated and experimented with the grounding datasets and multi-agent synthetic trajectories. She also performed extensive experiments on training and inference setups. Together with Tanmay and Piper, she shaped the training and evaluation codebases in the beginning and contributed throughout the project. Together with the team, she trained and evaluated the final models. 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Peter Sushko</span> led the synthetic data effort and model evaluation. He optimised the axtree data generation pipeline, produced synthetic tasks, collected the single-agent axtree and node traversal datasets, and developed data filtering strategies. Together with Piper Wolters he wrote much of the model evaluation code, focusing on web environments and large-scale distributed evaluation. He ran modeling ablations on dataset mixtures and ran evaluations for many baseline models.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rock Yuren Pang</span> led development of the demo and scaled it for broad public deployment, implementing safety guardrails to ensure responsible use and designing the human-AI interaction. He also played a key role in improving the human annotation tool, refining its initial implementation to enhance accuracy and streamline the human-in-the-loop workflow.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diego Llanes</span> created the Screenshot QA dataset and contributed to the task generation and trajectory filtering pipelines.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Yue Yang</span> explored synthetic data generation using code generation models and was involved in discussions related to data generation, training, and evaluation.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Taira Anderson</span> managed the project, resources, timelines and helped with cross-team communication.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Boyuan Zheng, Zhongzhen Ren, Harsh Trivedi</span> were involved in discussions related to training and evaluation.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Taylor Blanton</span> created the initial versions of the human annotation tool.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Caleb Ouellete</span> worked with Rock in setting up the required infrastructure for the demo.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Winson Han</span> created beautiful figures for this technical report.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ali Farhadi</span> advised the project.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="S7.SSx1.p2.1.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ranjay Krishna</span> was the PI for the project.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Overview</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this appendix, we provide the following:</p>
<ul id="A1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Details for human (<a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Human Trajectory Annotation ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>)and synthetic (<a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Synthetic Trajectories Generation ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>) trajectory generation pipelines, including details and prompts for how the tasks are sampled.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Additional dataset statistics like distribution of web categories, websites, and actions covered in <span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MolmoWebMix</span>. (<a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Additional Dataset Statistics ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>)</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Human Trajectory Annotation</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Annotation Tool</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Collecting high-accuracy human trajectories from the annotation tool (<a href="#A2.F7" title="In B.2.1 Manually written task templates. ‣ B.2 Task Sampling ‣ Appendix B Human Trajectory Annotation ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) is challenging due to various quirks of the Chrome extension, particularly around capturing screenshots along with DOM events. These timestamped events and screenshots were post-processed into a clean sequence of screenshots and user actions taken on those screenshots. Annotation workers were given detailed guidelines to ensure all important actions are captured. Particularly, the workers were asked to wait long enough after each action for the webpage to complete loading and for the annotation tool to trigger a screenshot automatically, or to manually take a screenshot in case an automatic screenshot is not triggered. Workers were also discouraged from acting too quickly to avoid missing events and screenshots via interventions like displaying a warning message and through annotation training. We partnered with Snorkel AI to scale-up the human annotations. Specifically, we provided tasks and our annotation tool to Snorkel AI who then managed the annotation workers, verified the annotations for correctness, and ensured quality control.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Task Sampling</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure a diversity of tasks for workers to annotate, we generate tasks using multiple strategies as described below:</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.1 </span>Manually written task templates.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To generate a core set of common use cases, authors wrote task templates. These include tasks related to shopping, news, real estate, travel (including flights, car rentals, hotels, etc.), maps, food &amp; recipes, job &amp; salary search, health &amp; wellness, and cars. Each task template consists of a sequence of atomic skills (using the taxonomy defined in Tab.1 in the main paper) with placeholders that are populated with samples drawn from predefined allowed constants (e.g., destinations for flight search) or sometimes generated on the fly (e.g., filters to apply while shopping for a product). Here’s an example for a shopping search and filter task:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><pre id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">go to: walgreens.com
search: coffee
apply filters: brand=Lavazza, availability=Pickup
find and open: most relevant product
</pre>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The annotation tool requires the workers to check each of these steps as they are completed. If a step can not be completed, the tool allows the worker to mark the step as incomplete along with a reason why the step could not be completed (e.g., a filter does not exist).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.08516v1/figures/fig-extension.jpg" id="A2.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/287;" width="476" height="287" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F7.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A2.F7.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Screenshot of the web browsing trajectory collection tool. The left half of the screen shows the webpage, the panel on the right is our chrome extension with annotations showing: <span id="A2.F7.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> last captured screenshot; <span id="A2.F7.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> instruction given to the annotator with a step-by-step breakdown; <span id="A2.F7.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c)</span> input box for leaving a note when marking a step could not be completed; <span id="A2.F7.8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d)</span> final answer.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For training purposes, in addition to these step-by-step instructions, we use an LLM to rewrite these instructions with different levels of specificity. The most specific low-level instruction is just a paraphrase of atomic steps into colloquial English, mid-level instruction is less verbose and could leave out details that may be obvious from context, and the highest-level instruction just states the intent without necessarily prescribing a way to achieve the intent. Here is an example of the different levels of specificity:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Low-level</span>: Go to walgreens.com, search for coffee, apply filters for Lavazza brand and available to pickup, and open the most relevant product.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mid-level</span>: On walgreens, search for Lavazza coffee available for pickup, and open the closest matching product.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">High-level</span>: Find Lavazza coffee for pickup at walgreens.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">During training, we randomly sample one of the 4 available instructions (steps-by-step and 3 levels) for each trajectory using a slightly higher sampling probability for the high-level instruction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.2 </span>LLM sampled tasks with steps.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To increase diversity, we also sample instructions using an LLM. We use a persona sampled from PersonaHub <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> to amplify task diversity along with the following prompt:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle" style="width:345.0pt;">

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to the manually written steps, we generate instructions at 3 levels of specificity for training from these LLM-sampled step-by-step tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.3 </span>LLM sampled tasks with navigation and QA.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While well structured and easy to follow, the tasks generated by the above prompt can be too rigid and may sometimes be infeasible (e.g., strict search filter constraints result in no matches on the website).
To generate more flexible tasks, for a portion of the tasks, we relax the constraint of generating sequence of atomic steps, and ask the LLM to generate a flexible request to navigate to a target webpage, followed by an optional question to be answered once on the target page. Here’s an example of such a task:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><pre id="A2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">navigate: Find Lavazza coffee for pickup on Walgreens
question: How much does it cost?
</pre>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The prompt used for sampling these navigation and QA tasks was as follows:</p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.4 </span>LLM sampled benchmark-like tasks.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All the above generation methods are agnostic to the target evaluation benchmarks and generally aim to cover diverse websites and tasks. However, the above approaches contain biases of authors (either directly in manually written templates or indirectly through prompts) that are likely to be different from the biases of the downstream benchmarks. Therefore, to close the gap in the distribution of tasks in the benchmarks, we generate a set of tasks using tasks from two of the four target benchmarks as in-context examples. Specifically, given a website and all tasks for that website from WebVoyager and Online-Mind2Web, we ask an LLM to generate tasks that are similar to the in-context examples, but not simply paraphrases.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use GPT-4o for the majority of the LLM sampled tasks, but for some tasks we cycle between GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5-mini, and GPT-5 to avoid biases of any single LLM and to increase task diversity.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Synthetic Trajectories Generation</h2>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Task Sampling</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sampling tasks for synthetic trajectories use the following strategies:</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.1 </span>Manually written task templates.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to manually written task templates for human annotation, a portion of tasks for generating trajectories are manually authored with detailed task templates. The main difference from the manual templates for human annotation is that these are natural language templates without a very well-defined atomic skill taxonomy. These manually written templates focused mainly on the websites in the WebVoyager benchmark.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.08516v1/figures/action_counts_histogram.jpg" id="A3.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/190;" width="476" height="190" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A3.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Action distribution breakdown across the dataset.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A3.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.08516v1/figures/website_sunburst.jpg" id="A3.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:429/429;" width="429" height="429" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A3.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Sunburst chart of domains and websites in the dataset.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.2 </span>LLM sampled benchmark-like tasks.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In a manner similar to the LLM sampled benchmark-like tasks for human annotations, we generated tasks that match the distribution of WebVoyager. For Online-Mind2Web, for a given task, instead of just generating tasks for the original website, with some probability, we sample a website from the same category (e.g., if the original website is a shopping website, we sample another shopping website from a pre-categorized list of websites), and ask an LLM to generate a similar task for that website.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.3 </span>Taxonomy-based tasks generation</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To enable generating diverse tasks and supplementing existing tasks, we define a comprehensive task taxonomy across four axes: (1) intent – what the user wants to do: info-seeking (looking up information), transactional (purchasing/booking), tool-use (using web tools to compute or create), messaging (sending messages or posting content), and navigation (reaching a specific page); (2) domain – the website category, spanning 13 areas: travel, ecommerce, productivity-apps, communication-apps, devtools, social, finance, education, media, reference, local, gov, and health; (3) difficulty – task complexity by constraint count: D0 (0–1 constraints), D1 (2–3), D2 (4–5), D3 (6+). Higher levels require satisfying more simultaneous requirements; (4) ambiguity – goal clarity and solution space: A0 (single correct answer), A1 (optimize under constraints, multiple valid solutions), A2 (open-ended comparison or recommendation), A3 (vague/underspecified goals needing clarification).</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We then develop a pipeline to generate synthetic web tasks by systematically iterating over this taxonomy. For each cell in the Cartesian product of these axes, it prompts an LLM (i.e., GPT-4o) to produce a specified number of diverse, realistic web browsing tasks. Each generated task includes a target website, a task type label, a sequence of concrete browser action steps, and three verbosity levels of natural language instructions (high-level, mid-level, low-level). The prompt constrains the LLM with detailed descriptions of each taxonomy axis value and optionally restricts website choices using a list of curated websites. Tasks are tagged with their taxonomy metadata during the generation process.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Additional Dataset Statistics</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across our synthetic and human datasets, a wide variety of web browsing domains and websites are covered. <a href="#A3.F9" title="In C.1.1 Manually written task templates. ‣ C.1 Task Sampling ‣ Appendix C Synthetic Trajectories Generation ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> presents a sunburst chart illustrating the hierarchical breakdown of broad web domains and websites represented in our training data, with just the top 9 websites for each category listed for readability. Our datasets are constructed to closely approximate the action space and input distribution characteristic of human web browsing behavior. In <a href="#A3.F8" title="In C.1.1 Manually written task templates. ‣ C.1 Task Sampling ‣ Appendix C Synthetic Trajectories Generation ‣ MolmoWeb: Open Visual Web Agent and Open Data for the Open Web" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> we show the distribution of actions across our various training datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
</div>
